# Session — 2026-05-14 — taking over the bakery

Teller: Els. Interviewer: Jip.

We took over the bakery on the Vissersdijk in 1978. Your father signed the papers with flour already on his sleeves, that is how sure he was. I was twenty-six and I had never once seen four o'clock in the morning.

The front of the shop was ice until the ovens caught up. Cold, then warm — that was the whole day. I kneaded with my coat on until six. The smell of the first proof is the smell I will want on my last day. Yeast and warm linen.

The harbor men came at five thirty, before anyone else was awake. They never spoke before the first roll, not one word, and I learned not to speak either. Mrs. Terpstra came every Thursday for the raisin loaf and paid in coins she counted twice.

[Jip's note: she got up mid-session to find the shop bell in the box under the stairs. Held it the rest of the hour.]

# Session — 2026-06-02 — the strike year

Teller: Els. Interviewer: Jip.

The strike year was bad. I will not dress it up. Nineteen eighty-four, the flour price doubled in one season and we did not sleep for the mathematics of it. Your father wanted to sell. I said the ovens stay lit.

I took in mending in the afternoons so they could stay lit. Nobody in the town knew. I did the mending in the back room with the curtain closed, and I hid the sewing basket in the flour store when customers came through to the back. Mrs. Terpstra nearly caught me twice.

You were four that year. You slept in the flour sacks like a cat. The customers asked after you like you were part of the inventory.

What I remember best from the bad year is the morning your father hung the strike poster in the window and then baked for the strikers anyway, free, before dawn, so no one would see them take the bread. He never once called it charity. He called it keeping the ovens honest.

# Session — 2026-06-21 — the shop, start to finish

Teller: Els. Interviewer: Jip.

We opened the doors in the spring of 1979 — I remember because the tulip men still had their stalls out when we swept the front the first time. [Jip's note: session 1 says 1978; she was certain both times. Did the papers get signed in 1978 and the doors open later? Not resolved.]

The wedding cakes were my department. I made forty-one wedding cakes in twelve years. I counted, because each one went up in the window on the Friday and the whole street came to look. The one I never got to make was for my sister Riet. She called off the wedding two weeks before, and the fruit was already soaking. We ate the fruit at Christmas for three years and never once said what it was for.

My hands ended it, mostly. And the supermarket on the ring road, a little. We sold in 1990 to the Boonstra boy, who let it become a phone shop, which I have decided not to be bitter about. I kept the shop bell. When I shake it I am twenty-six again, cold then warm.
